text: The inner product gave you a way to measure overlap between states. The next question is what kind of matrix is allowed to represent something you can actually measure — an energy, a spin, a position. The answer is Hermitian, and it connects directly to a fact you rely on every day: measurement results are real numbers, never complex ones.

A matrix's conjugate transpose is formed by transposing it and conjugating every entry. A matrix is Hermitian if it equals its own conjugate transpose, which for a 2 by 2 matrix means two things: the diagonal entries must be real, and the off-diagonal entries must be conjugates of each other.

Take A equals 2, 1 minus 2i, 1 plus 2i, negative 1. Its diagonal is real, and conjugating 1 minus 2i gives 1 plus 2i, which matches exactly — Hermitian. Now take B equals 1, 2 plus i, 3 minus i, 4. The diagonal is real, but conjugating 2 plus i gives 2 minus i, which does not match 3 minus i — B is not Hermitian, even though its diagonal looked fine. Both conditions have to pass.

For that same matrix A, the trace is 1 and the determinant works out to negative 7. Solving the characteristic equation gives eigenvalues of roughly 3.19 and negative 2.19 — both real numbers, even though A itself has complex off-diagonal entries. That's not a coincidence of this particular matrix; it's a theorem: every Hermitian matrix has only real eigenvalues.

In quantum mechanics, every measurable quantity — energy, spin, position — is represented by a Hermitian operator, because a measurement result has to come out as an ordinary real number; you can't get 3 plus 2i joules off a real measuring device. Hermitian matrices are precisely the ones guaranteed to have real eigenvalues no matter how complex-looking the matrix itself is, which is exactly why they're the only matrices that can safely represent something you physically measure.

Next lesson looks at a different kind of operator — one that represents not what you measure, but how a quantum state is allowed to evolve, including every gate in a circuit — and the specific algebraic condition every one of those gate matrices must satisfy.
